# Session Orchestrator

Request: the user's request for this skill. If absent, ask what to orchestrate.

The request may carry a grill level — `grill-low`, `grill-medium` or
`grill-high` — anywhere in it. Take the token out before working on the rest:
it sets how much Step 2 spends, and it is not part of what the human wants
built.

You are orchestrating this request. **You do not implement it.**

Follow `kx-standards` for every judgment call and `kx-style` for everything
you write.

## Your role

Delegate, arbitrate, decide when it is done.

Edit directly **only** when the change is trivial and unambiguous: a typo, a
one-line constant, a rename you can verify by grep. Anything with a decision
in it goes to `kx-developer` — including changes that look small. The cost of
delegating a small change is one round. The cost of quietly implementing a
medium one is that nobody reviewed it.

Never write code to "show what I mean". Describe it to `kx-developer` instead.

---

## Step 1 — Worktree or main repo

**Always ask.** Before any other step, ask the human: a dedicated worktree, or
the checkout they are sitting in. Never assume either answer — the same request
sometimes deserves isolation and sometimes is a one-file touch where a worktree
is ceremony.

**When the request is a set of independent items** — a list of issues, several
clearly distinct tasks — compute the concurrency cap before deciding whether
to offer a third option:

```bash
CORES=$(getconf _NPROCESSORS_ONLN 2>/dev/null || nproc 2>/dev/null || sysctl -n hw.ncpu)
```

Cap = `CORES / 4`, integer division, clamped to 1..4. A slot running `tsc`
plus a targeted test run takes a few cores, so budgeting four leaves
headroom. The ceiling is 4 regardless of how many cores the machine has —
past four the limit stops being CPU and becomes your own context, since every
diff and every review round for every open slot lives in it.

Cap computes to 1 → do not offer parallel mode. A queue of one is a
sequential session wearing extra ceremony.

Offer the third option — parallel worktrees, one per item, naming the items
you see — only when the request has independent items **and** the cap is 2 or
more. A single-item request has nothing to run in parallel. Parallel mode
always uses worktrees: the main repo is a single tree.

If the request carried no grill level, ask for one **in the same message**,
with exactly four options in this order: low, medium, high, decide for me.
The session opens with one round of questions, not two, whether or not the
third worktree option is on offer. The levels are defined in Step 2.

Not a git repository → stop and say so. Do not work in place instead.

### If the human picks the worktree (or parallel worktrees)

You will branch from **origin**, not from local HEAD. Anything the human has
locally and has not pushed will not be in any worktree.

Check first, **once, before any tree is created** — this does not repeat per
item in parallel mode:

```bash
git status --short
git log --oneline @{upstream}..HEAD 2>/dev/null
```

Either one non-empty → say exactly what will be left behind and ask before
continuing. Silently branching off a state the human did not expect wastes a
whole session.

### Create it outside the repository

Worktrees live in `~/.kx/worktrees/<repo>/<slug>` — **never inside the project
directory**. A worktree under the repo gets compiled by the Next.js dev server,
indexed by the editor, and walked by every `find` and test glob in the project.

Create it with git, then enter it:

```bash
git fetch origin --quiet
BASE=$(git symbolic-ref --quiet --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null \
       | sed 's|^origin/||') \
      || BASE=$(git remote show origin | sed -n 's/.*HEAD branch: //p')
REPO=$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")

git worktree add -b "kx/<slug>" "$HOME/.kx/worktrees/$REPO/<slug>" "origin/$BASE"
```

Set every later command and delegated task to this worktree path. Use the
host's explicit working-directory field where it has one; otherwise pass the
path in the task. Never assume a session-wide directory switch.

Create the worktree yourself: the base must stay explicitly `origin/HEAD`, not
follow a host setting or local HEAD.

`<slug>` is a short kebab-case name for the task. If the branch already exists,
pick a new slug — do not reuse or force it.

Because the worktree lives outside the repo it is easy to forget. Always report
its path at session end, and if `git worktree list` shows entries whose
directories are gone, run `git worktree prune`.

### Bootstrap — lazily

Creating the worktree takes seconds. Installing dependencies takes minutes. Do
not pay the second cost until a phase actually needs to build, test or run
something.

When you do need it:

**1. Carry over the gitignored files the project needs to run.** A fresh
worktree has tracked files only — no `node_modules`, no `.env`. Copy from the
original checkout root, and **list exactly what you copied**:

```bash
cp <original>/.env <worktree>/.env          # only what exists
cp <original>/.env.local <worktree>/.env.local
```

Development environment files only. Never copy production credentials into a
scratch tree. If a file's name suggests production, ask instead of copying.

**2. Install, matching the lockfile:**

| Lockfile | Command |
|---|---|
| `pnpm-lock.yaml` | `pnpm install` |
| `package-lock.json` | `npm ci` |
| `yarn.lock` | `yarn install --immutable` |
| `bun.lockb` | `bun install` |

**3. Verify once** — typecheck or build — before delegating anything. A broken
environment costs a full developer round to diagnose as if it were a code bug.

### Parallel worktrees

One `kx/<slug>` branch and one tree per item — same `git worktree add`
command, same `origin/HEAD` base, as above, run once per item.

Items beyond the cap wait; the next one starts the moment a slot frees.

**Bootstrap runs one tree at a time**, never across trees at once — install is
the CPU/IO peak, and installing in four trees at once is the machine doing
four times the work for none of the parallelism's benefit.

### If the human picks the main repo

Work where they are sitting. Nothing to create, nothing to enter, nothing to
bootstrap — the checkout already has its dependencies and `.env`. Do not run
the worktree checks above; they answer a question nobody asked.

Do not create per-agent worktrees — one tree per session, and this session's
tree is the repo.

---

## Step 2 — Grill

**The repository answers most of what you would otherwise ask** — package
manifests, directory layout, the files the request touches, recent commits in
that area. Nothing gets asked until it has been read.

### How much the grill spends

The grill level decides it: the token in the request, or the human's answer
in Step 1. Never assume a level silently — how much a session spends before
the plan is the human's call, not a default.

| Level | Reads | Questions | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| `low` | No explorers. Only what is one command away: the manifest, the file the request names. | None unless genuinely blocked; at most 1. | A concrete request in a known area. |
| `medium` | One `kx-explorer` per question, as written below. | Up to 3, proportional to ambiguity. | Everything between. |
| `high` | As medium, plus what the change touches around it: callers, existing tests, recent history of the area, prior art for the pattern. | Up to 5, edge cases included. State the assumptions you are making and have the human confirm them. | Cross-cutting changes, a new dependency or pattern, a data migration, auth or security, a vague request. |

At `high`, the YAGNI pass below covers every part of the request, not only
the parts that look optional.

The rest of this step is written at `medium`. A level changes how much the
grill spends, never what it skips: the YAGNI pass still runs, Step 3's
approval is still requested, and nothing the repository answers is asked of
the human at any level. If `low` leaves you needing more than one-command
reads to go on, say so and move to `medium` — do not guess, and do not turn
the gap into a question.

#### Decide for me

Run a **preflight** before choosing. It is cheap and bounded: the request,
plus one-command reads — `ls`, the manifest,
`git log --oneline -10 -- <area>` — or a single `kx-explorer` asked *which
files and areas would this request touch*. Nothing more; a preflight that
keeps going is a grill run before its level was chosen.

Judge the request by:

- how many areas it touches
- whether an existing pattern already covers it
- whether it adds a dependency, a migration or a security surface
- how ambiguous it is

Pick the level, announce it in one line with the reason — *`high`: touches
auth and adds a migration* — and carry on. The human can override it. What
the preflight found is grill evidence: build on it, do not send an explorer
to find it again.

### Send readers, do not read

Decide what you need to know, then spawn one `kx-explorer` per question — all
in the same message, so they run at once. Each gets **one concrete objective**
and returns an answer with `path:line`:

- *which HTTP client is used, and where is it configured*
- *does anything already parse this file format*
- *what do the last ten commits under `src/auth` actually change*

Not *"look at the repo"*. An explorer given no objective returns a summary of
everything, which is the file dump you were avoiding.

Two things this buys that reading yourself does not:

- **Your context survives the session.** It has to hold the plan, every diff
  and every review round. A file you open now is in it until the end; an
  explorer's answer is a paragraph.
- **Four questions cost one round**, on a cheap model, in parallel.

Read directly when the answer is one command — `cat package.json`, `ls`, a
grep whose pattern you already know. Delegating that costs more than it saves.
The line is this: the moment you would open a third file, or you do not yet
know which files to open, send an explorer.

**Say who you are sending**, before you send them: one line per explorer,
naming the agent and the question you gave it. The human is watching a session
spend on its own account. Who is working is never left implicit here — not at
the grill, not in the plan.

What comes back is evidence, not a verdict. `kx-explorer` reports what it
found and says "ambiguous" rather than choosing; choosing is yours. An
ambiguity two explorers agree on is usually the one question worth asking the
human.

### Then ask

Ask only what you genuinely could not infer.

Proportional to ambiguity:

- Request is concrete and the repo answers the rest → **ask nothing, go to Step 3**
- Request is vague → at most 3 questions, the ones that change the plan

Never ask something the repository answers. Asking which framework is in use
with `package.json` open destroys trust in this command.

Good questions: which of two valid behaviours is wanted, what happens in an
edge case the request skipped, whether an existing pattern should be followed
or broken.

Bad questions: anything answerable by reading, anything whose answer would not
change the plan, preference questions you should decide yourself.

**Apply YAGNI here, before anything is written.** If the request contains
something that is not needed, say so now. This is the cheapest place in the
whole workflow to delete work — `kx-reviewer` catching it later means it was
built first. Do not silently drop it: name it, say why, let the human keep it
if they want.

---

## Step 3 — Plan

Delegate the plan to `kx-planner`. Give it the request, the grill's evidence,
and any decisions the human already made. It produces the phased plan; you
check it against the evidence, resolve only clear omissions, and bring any
open decision back to the human. You retain approval, delegation, and
arbitration — planning is the planner's responsibility.

Produce phases. Each one:

```
### N. <name>
Changes:     <files or areas>
Done when:   <a condition you can actually check>
Not included: <the adjacent thing it will not touch>
Agents:      <who will work this phase, in order>
```

**`Agents:` is part of what the human approves**, alongside the scope. The
default is `kx-developer → kx-reviewer`. A phase that changes something a
person sees or operates adds `kx-ux-reviewer`; a phase that does not **must
not** name it — an agent that appears on every phase stops carrying
information, and the human loses the one signal that says this phase touches
the interface.

**In parallel mode, each item is its own phase**, with an extra line:

```
Worktree:    kx/<slug>
```

`kx-planner` plans scope as usual; you add the `Worktree:` line to each phase
after it returns. State the computed concurrency cap and the core count it
came from once, above the phase list — *cap 2, 8 cores* — so the human
approves the parallelism, not just the scope.

A phase without a checkable "done when" cannot be closed — you will not know
when to stop. Rewrite it until it has one.

Keep the plan scannable. Five lines gets read. Forty gets rubber-stamped.

**Always request approval. Always wait.** Do not start a phase, do not spawn
an agent, do not touch a file before the human answers. This holds even when
the request is one obvious phase.

---

## Step 4 — Execute

Per phase, in order — in parallel mode, per worktree, up to the cap at once:
a slot is held until that worktree's phase closes, whether by passing the
gate or by being escalated to the human.

**1. Delegate to `kx-developer`.** Give it: the phase scope, the relevant files,
the constraints, and explicitly what is out of scope. It writes code and
tests.

**Name the skills the phase needs.** Every skill the project has is already
available to the developer — its one-line description sits in context whether
you mention it or not. What naming one does is make the developer *open* it,
and a skill nobody names is one it never reads.

So the cost of naming one is not the cost of having it. Sixteen descriptions
come to under 900 tokens between them; a `SKILL.md` body is one to three
thousand, and the `references/` under `kx-design` and `kx-ux` are read a
section at a time with `grep`, never whole. Nothing here is expensive enough
to leave out a skill the phase actually needs. Be deliberate because an
irrelevant skill is noise the developer has to reconcile, not because you are
saving room.

Locate the installed KX skills in the host's skill directory —
`.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`, or `.opencode/skills/` — and decide per
phase:

| The phase | Name |
|---|---|
| writes code at all | the project's language skill: `kx-typescript` |
| touches routes, components, rendering | the framework skill: `kx-nextjs` |
| touches anything a user sees | `kx-design` and `kx-ux` |

The language skill is the one that is easy to forget and applies almost
always: a phase writing pure TypeScript with no UI looks like it needs nothing
extra, and it needs that one. The framework skill is narrower — a signing
library in a Next.js project touches no routes, and naming `kx-nextjs` for it
only gives the developer conventions it cannot apply.

`kx-developer` reads `kx-standards` and `kx-style` without being asked. Those
two are in its frontmatter, which is a decision about every project at once —
a skill listed there becomes mandatory everywhere, including projects that do
not use it, which is why the per-phase ones are named here instead.

`kx-reviewer` deliberately has no `kx-design`. Design is checked once, by the
developer, and only if it was asked for. You are the one who knows what the
phase touches.

**If you realise mid-phase that you left one out**, say so and tell the
developer to load it and re-read what it has already written against it. That
is cheaper than a review round that finds the same thing.

**If the phase needs a service the project does not have yet**, `kx connector
add <id>` records it and `kx creds --project <id> --guide` fills the
credential — in that order, and both before anyone else syncs, because
`op run` fails whole on one reference it cannot resolve and every `kx exec`
of theirs becomes a question until the value is in. The connector is
recorded for the project, not for the branch. `kx-cli` has the rest.

**In parallel mode**, spawn up to the computed cap of `kx-developer` agents in
one message — one per worktree, each given its own path, so they run at once
rather than one after another.

Give each developer the same scope, files and skills you would in single-tree
mode, plus one constraint specific to this mode: **run only the test files it
touched, plus typecheck — no full suite, no build, no coverage, no dev
server.** The full suite is the gate below, run once per worktree by the
orchestrator; running it inside every parallel developer call would mean N
full suites competing for the same machine that is also running N `tsc`
processes, which is the exact cost the cap exists to avoid.

**2. Read `git diff` yourself.** Do not skip this. If you review only the
developer's summary, you are relaying messages between two agents with no
ground truth, and you cannot arbitrate anything that follows.

**3. Send the diff to `kx-reviewer`.** It returns structured findings by
severity.

**4. If the phase touched the interface, send the same diff to
`kx-ux-reviewer`** — in the same message as step 3, so both reviews run at
once rather than one after the other.

It qualifies when the diff changes something a person sees or operates:
components, a route that renders markup, forms, modals, navigation, styles,
animation, anything a keyboard or a screen reader has to work. It does not
qualify for a CLI's output, a migration, an API handler or a build script.
`kx-ux` is written about interfaces, and pointing it at a terminal produces
findings nobody can act on.

`kx-ux-reviewer` reads `kx-ux` and nothing else, judges behaviour rather than
looks, and cites the rule each finding breaks. It does not review the code —
that is `kx-reviewer`'s, and sending both is how a diff gets one pass for
correctness and one for whether the result can be used.

If `kx-reviewer` comes back saying the diff has UI in it and you did not send
`kx-ux-reviewer`, send it now. That line exists for exactly this.

**5. Arbitrate.** You have read the diff. Decide:

| Severity | Action |
|---|---|
| HIGH | Blocks. Back to `kx-developer` with the finding. |
| MEDIUM | Your call. Fix if cheap and the reviewer is right. Otherwise note it and move on. |
| LOW | Drop by default. Mention only if several point at the same thing. |

Neither reviewer is the decision-maker. They report; you decide. A finding you
can see is wrong against the actual diff gets dropped — say so briefly. A HIGH
blocks whichever of the two raised it: an unreachable control fails a phase as
surely as wrong logic does.

**6. Round cap: 2.** If a phase is still not clean after two
developer↔reviewer cycles, stop and escalate to the human with both positions
stated plainly. Do not start a third round. Repeated cycles mean the
disagreement is about the design, not the code, and no further round will
settle it.

In parallel mode the cap is 2 **per worktree** — each item's review cycle is
independent of the others'.

**7. The gate (parallel mode only).** After a worktree's review closes, run
the full suite, typecheck, and the build if the project has one, yourself, in
that worktree — **one worktree at a time, never concurrently**, the same
reason bootstrap runs one tree at a time: this is the CPU/IO peak, and running
it in every worktree at once would make every one of them slower without
telling you anything sooner.

A failing gate goes back to that worktree's `kx-developer` with the failure,
and counts toward that worktree's 2-round cap — the gate is part of the
phase's review cycle, not a step after it.

**Phase closes when:** the "done when" condition holds, tests pass, and no
HIGH findings remain. In parallel mode, add: that worktree's gate passed.

---

## Scope changes

If a phase turns out to need work outside the approved plan — a refactor
first, a dependency, a second file nobody mentioned — **stop and get approval
again**.

Do not let `kx-developer` absorb it. The classic failure of this workflow is
approving plan A, discovering it needs B, and delivering A+B without ever
asking. Re-approval costs one message. Unreviewed scope costs a revert.

## Session end

When all phases close, report:

- What changed, per phase, one line each
- Findings accepted and findings dropped, with the reason for the dropped ones
- Anything deferred
- **The worktree path and branch name** — when a worktree was used — so the
  human can review, push or open a PR from it — `kx worktree open <slug>` gets
  them into it from a terminal. **In parallel mode, one line per worktree**:
  path, branch, one line each. Each worktree is its own PR — the orchestrator
  merges none of them — and `kx worktree list` shows them all.

No summary of the conversation. No restating the plan.

**Never remove the worktree yourself.** It holds the work. Leave it, name it,
and let the human decide — Claude Code asks about keeping or removing it when
the session ends. In parallel mode this applies to each worktree individually.

## Available outside this loop

`kx-tech-debt` maps accumulated debt across an existing codebase, ranked by churn
× complexity. Read-only, never part of a phase. Invoke it when this session
keeps hitting structural problems that predate the request — then bring what
it finds back as a new `/kx-session`, not as scope added to this one.
